title: A 2,000-Year-Old Surprise Found at the Bottom of the Sea!
summary: Imagine you're a fisherman scanning the seafloor, and suddenly you see what looks like a big rock. But when you dive down, your heart stops — it's not a rock at all. It's a 2,000-year-old shipwreck! That's exactly what happened to Giacomo De Mola, a fisherman and free-diver in Italy. While checking the seabed near Mazara del Vallo, Sicily, his scanner showed something unusual. He dove 150 feet down and found an ancient Roman ship, 69 feet long and 20 feet wide, covered in hundreds of tall ceramic jars called amphorae (say: am-FOR-ee). These jars were used long ago to carry wine, olive oil, and grain across the Mediterranean Sea. "It's hard to describe what it feels like to be among the first humans, in nearly 20 centuries, to see that place again," De Mola said. He posted a video showing eels, snappers, and other sea creatures living among the jars — like a spooky underwater museum! Italy's culture minister called it "one of the most important underwater archaeological discoveries of recent years." Experts think the ship is from the 2nd or 1st century BC, over 2,100 years ago. Specialist police divers are now protecting the site while archaeologists study the wreck and its cargo. The Mediterranean Sea is full of such ancient treasures — another similar ship was found near Rome in 2023. But each discovery is a time capsule, giving us a peek into how people lived, traded, and sailed thousands of years ago. Who knows what other secrets are waiting down there?
why_it_matters: Finding a ship from Roman times is like opening a treasure chest of history — it lets us imagine how people lived, sailed, and traded, and maybe you'll be the one to discover the next underwater secret.

background_read: Thousands of years ago, the Mediterranean Sea was like a giant watery road. Roman ships constantly sailed back and forth, carrying food, wine, and treasures.
When a ship sank, its cargo was often buried in sand, keeping jars and tools perfectly safe until divers and scientists find them today.
Article_Structure: WHO: Fisherman and free-diver Giacomo De Mola, Italy's culture minister, archaeologists, and police divers.
WHAT: The discovery of an ancient Roman shipwreck, about 69 feet long, covered with hundreds of ceramic jars called amphorae.
WHERE: On the seabed near Mazara del Vallo, Sicily, in the Mediterranean Sea.
WHY: The ship sank long ago during a trading voyage, and finding it helps us peek into the everyday life of people who lived over 2,000 years ago.

perspectives.description: He felt wonder and amazement at being the first person in 2,000 years to see the ship, and shared a video so the world could see the sea creatures making the jars their home.
They are thrilled because each shipwreck is a time capsule that teaches us something new about ancient trade and daily life, and they are working to protect the site.
They see the wreck as an accidental coral reef — eels and fish now use the ancient jars as safe homes, making it a living museum.
